Empirical Results · Public-Data Spine (v2, caveats addressed)

AI Workload Power Shaping — Results on Real Public Data

End-to-end implementation and evaluation on real measured data: the emerald 256-GPU DVFS sweep and its real grid-experiment power traces, the 27.3M-request Azure LLM trace, and the Zeus power-limit sweeps across heterogeneous workloads. The model is validated against a real field experiment; every headline number is read from a saved artifact behind a passing invariant.

Bottom line

Workload-aware power shaping delivers material, validated decision value over uniform capping and priority-only scheduling. The value is regime- and heterogeneity-dependent — small when curtailment is shallow and workloads are similar, large when curtailment is deep or the fleet is heterogeneous — and the model reproduces a real field experiment to within 0.062 per workload.

■The systems view — grid stress to service to rebound

One time-aligned figure ties the spine together: an Israeli evening grid-stress scenario sets a power allowance; the backlog-aware controller shapes facility power to it using a mix of GPU power-capping and deferral; per-class latency shows critical/interactive protected while deferrable work is delayed; and the deferred backlog drains into a bounded rebound after the event. Panels 3–6 are the PoC-B tick simulator run on the real Azure trace + measured emerald elasticity (simulated-on-measured); panels 1–2 are the grid scenario.

Measured closed-loop control on a real GPU

To ground the control claim in hardware — not simulation — we ran a closed-loop duty-cycle controller on a real AWS g5.xlarge (A10G). A latency-sensitive stream and a deferrable throughput job share the GPU; a power target steps down during a constrained window and the controller regulates the deferrable duty cycle so measured NVML power tracks the target.

Measured — control claim grounded on hardware

In the constrained window, the controller holds measured GPU power at 171 W against a 165 W target (uncontrolled draws 299 W, over by 134 W), while critical p95 latency stays at 14.51 ms and the deferrable job is throttled (58.0→19.0 it/s). Panel 3 of the systems figure — simulated on the measured elasticity — is therefore backed by a real hardware control loop, not simulation alone.

◉How the model is used — dataflow

The response model is a feedforward predictor the controller queries every tick: given a candidate action (a GPU power-cap fraction and per-class admit/defer gates), it predicts the facility power and serving throughput that action would produce. The controller picks the least-shedding action whose predicted power stays under the grid allowance C(t), then closes the loop on the measured power signal. The model is trained offline on measured elasticity; it is deliberately simple (a class-mean / physically-grounded form) because the data spans only ~14 distinct workloads, where a deep model overfits (see §6).

Action space: continuous GPU power cap (public elasticity data) and batching (own data). Service cost = ∑ priority-weight × throughput loss. Oracle: exact multiple-choice-knapsack DP cross-checked against water-filling and SLSQP. Every experiment carries a sanity invariant that had to pass before its numbers were kept.

2PoC-A — the kill test

Does selecting workloads by measured power elasticity beat simple policies? Continuous allocation on a 40-job pool from the 8 measured emerald workloads.

Kill criterion A1 — cleared

Oracle improves service cost by 17–32% over uniform capping across 10–30% curtailment (kill threshold ~5%). Profiled greedy achieves the oracle. On these similar LLM workloads the gain is mostly priority-weighted spreading (98% captured by priority + average elasticity); naive priority-first is a trap.

3Validation against a real field experiment

During the emerald SRP grid experiment the real 256-GPU cluster cut power 32% and recorded per-workload service performance. We ask our allocator to hit the same reduction on the same workloads and compare predicted vs measured performance — a test, not a fit.

Power-model realism — addressed

The allocator's per-workload choices match a real grid experiment to 0.062, and it is slightly conservative on aggregate performance (model 0.824 ≤ field 0.886) — the safe direction for a grid-facing system.

4Real heterogeneity — when per-workload elasticity matters

The emerald data is LLM-only and near-homogeneous. The Zeus power-limit sweeps give real heterogeneous workloads (vision, recommendation, speech, NLP), replacing the earlier surrogate.

Real finding that corrects the intuition

The memory-bound recommendation workload (NCF) draws only ~37 W regardless of the power cap (100→250 W) — it already runs far below any cap, so power-capping sheds nothing from it. Flexible power lives in the compute-bound workloads, and per-workload value comes from their differing cap-sensitivity — not from a memory-bound "free lunch" as a naive model would assume.

Per-workload elasticity value across four real datasets

The same decomposition on four independent real DVFS/power-cap datasets spanning GPU and CPU, ML and HPC. Per-workload elasticity carries decision value in every one — the result is not an artifact of any single benchmark.

Own-measured intervention-response & cross-hardware (Gate ⅠⅠⅠ progress)

Reusing 346 past Modal runs across 7 real GPUs (T4…H100, H200): batching is a real power-shaping actuator — a batch-aware controller beats uniform by 72% (per-workload value 31%), since datacenter GPUs are batch-elastic while T4/L4 are flat. The unseen-hardware (S3) model predicts a held-out GPU's power to MAE 38 W vs a 187 W global-mean baseline — real cross-hardware generalization on own data. A power-cap sweep needs a root pod (vast/RunPod): a Modal probe confirmed its containers cannot set power limits or lock clocks.

5PoC-B — real Azure inference replay

Does the advantage survive realistic arrivals? A 1-second-tick serving simulator replays the real Azure busy hour under a dynamic envelope; a backlog-aware feedforward controller holds power under C(t).

Finding — regime-dependent value

At shallow-to-moderate curtailment, uniform capping suffices and workload-aware shaping matches it. At deep curtailment (firm cap ≤ ~50% of peak) it cuts weighted service cost by 94× (344,387→3,672) and holds critical-class SLO violations at 0% vs uniform's 42%.

6Learned controller, Oracle Capture & safety

A learned controller must pick good interventions for workloads it has not profiled. Leave-one-workload-out: predict each workload's response from features, allocate optimally on the predictions, score on the true curves.

Oracle Capture (unseen workloads)

Leakage-free (held-out workload excluded from its own family mean), a learned class model recovers 77% of the oracle's advantage on homogeneous emerald, but on heterogeneous Zeus (only 6 workloads, mostly unique families) it fails (worse than uniform) — it cannot learn the compute-vs-memory split from so few examples. GBDT overfits worse still. This is why the safety promise uses a physical bound, not the learned model (next card), and why more diverse workloads are the lever (§6.1).

Safe flexibility (RQ6, resolved)

47% of naive per-workload promises under-deliver, and statistical intervals do not help (47%) — the failures are out-of-distribution. Fix: a physical ceiling from one runtime power reading (shed ≤ current draw−cap) drives under-delivery to 0% while still promising 70% of the real flexibility.

Rebound control

Uncontrolled recovery sustains +35% over baseline; a recovery cap cuts it to -13% — peak shaving without relocating the peak.

6.1What improves the model — tested by collecting data

The learned model fails on heterogeneous workloads when there are too few of them (Zeus, 6 workloads, above). Is the bottleneck the model or the data? Two checks say data: perfect-information capture is 100% (invariant-verified — given the true curves the allocator matches the oracle, so the headroom is real), and on the hard case model-side levers give no lift (an observed compute-intensity feature and a light 2-point elasticity probe both +0; a deeper GBDT overfits and loses to the simple class model). So we tested the data hypothesis directly: we spent ~$1 on the self-cleaning AWS harness to measure 26 diverse workloads (GEMM/conv/attention/FFT through memory-bound gather/reduction/softmax, a 13× sheddable-power range) on one real A10G — a consistent construct where we control the workload count.

Result — more distinct workloads turn failure into a working model

Leakage-free Oracle Capture rises with the number of workloads on this single construct, from -133% at 6 workloads (a failure, like Zeus at the same scale) to 48% at 26 workloads — and the run-to-run variance collapses (sd 122→0). The prescription “more distinct, diverse workloads at a consistent construct” is therefore not just a diagnosis: collecting them for ~$1 measurably moved a heterogeneous case from worse-than-uniform to 48% of the oracle. The harness (AWS power-cap + Modal batching) scales this to more workloads and GPUs on demand.

Honesty note (correction): an earlier version reported Oracle Capture 83%/38% (emerald/Zeus) using a class-mean that averaged each held-out workload into its own family mean — leakage. Corrected leakage-free, the numbers are 77% (emerald) and Zeus fails (worse than uniform); the AWS learning curve above is computed with the same corrected, leakage-free estimator. Caveat on “just add rows”: the workloads must be genuinely diverse within one construct — naively pooling two separable hardware families inflates capture through family separability, not learning.

7Firm capacity — CCM, real priorities, and the Israel case

Compute Capacity Multiplier

Behind the same firm capacity, workload-aware shaping supports 5.0× installed compute vs uniform's 1.8× (balanced synthetic mix, inference serving).

Reality check with REAL priorities

On the Alibaba spot trace (466k jobs, real HP/Spot labels), the opportunistic fraction at peak is only 4%, giving CCM 1.04× from priority labels alone — far below the inference CCM, which counted a larger deferrable fraction. Priority-first always protects HP power ≥ uniform (invariant). The true firm-capacity gain depends strongly on how much work is genuinely flexible.

Israel firm-capacity case study (ministry-facing)

The spec's IL-2 evening-constraint scenario on a 100 MW virtual facility, against a representative Israeli summer day. Motivating context: the Israel Electricity Authority reported a ~27 GW data-center connection queue and paused new ≥8 MVA connections (July 2026).

Firm-capacity result

Under the IL-2 evening constraint, 100 MW of installed AI compute operates behind a 75 MW firm cap while fully protecting critical load and meeting the envelope — the "third option" between approving 100 MW and rejecting the project. Value is contingent on the flexible-workload fraction (see the real-priority reality check).

8Verification — invariants & bugs caught

InvariantExpectationStatus
PoC-A INV-1 / INV-2Oracle ≤ every heuristic; homogeneous pool → ~0 headroompass
PoC-B INV-B1 / INV-B2Unconstrained → no shedding; binding → uniform critical SLO ≥ prioritypass
Field validationModel conservative vs measured field performancepass
Model / CCMGBDT ≤ mean on seen data; CCM(elasticity) ≥ CCM(uniform)pass
Bugs the invariants / investigations caught & fixed
  • Infeasible oracle faking headroom (bucket rounding) → round power up, cross-check vs SLSQP.
  • Jitter plateau giving the oracle free shed power → preserve the measured curve shape.
  • Tick vs deadline masking the comparison → 0.5 s tick, meetable deadlines.
  • Free-priority serve handing uniform the benefit → class-blind uniform serves FIFO.
  • Controller over-shedding at mild dips → cap-through-range ladder, elasticity ≥ uniform everywhere.
  • NCF "free lunch" assumption → real data shows memory-bound NCF draws ~37 W flat, no flexibility.
